title: Grand Hotel
events_chronological: Doctor Otternschlag, whose face was ruined in the war, sits in the lobby telling anyone who passes that people come and go and nothing ever happens.
Otto Kringelein, a bookkeeper who has been told he is dying, cashes in his savings and takes the most expensive room in the hotel.
Baron von Gaigern, a ruined nobleman working as a hotel thief, is pressed by his creditors for money he does not have.
The industrialist Preysing arrives to close a merger that will collapse unless he lies about it.
The ballerina Grusinskaya refuses to go on, saying that nobody comes to see her dance any more.
Preysing engages the stenographer Flaemmchen and makes plain what else the position involves.
The Baron hides in Grusinskaya's room to take her pearls and instead spends the night listening to her.
Grusinskaya finds him there, and the two of them are in love by morning.
Kringelein loses his temper with Preysing, who is his own employer, in the bar and tells him exactly what he thinks of him.
The Baron takes up with Kringelein and teaches him to drink and to dance.
Grusinskaya dances better than she has in years and arranges to leave for Vienna with the Baron in the morning.
Kringelein wins heavily at cards and then loses his wallet, and the Baron, who has stolen it, gives it back to him.
Preysing's merger collapses when the truth about the English deal comes out.
The Baron breaks into Preysing's room for the money, and Preysing beats him to death with a telephone.
Preysing is arrested, Grusinskaya leaves for the station believing the Baron will follow, Kringelein takes Flaemmchen away with him, and Otternschlag repeats that nothing ever happens.
syuzhet_notes: The film moves from room to room across two days in one building, so consecutive told-order bullets belong to different guests rather than to different times.
fabula_notes: The two days are continuous. Where two guests are doing things at the same hour, either order would do.
